drills.q: Why doesn't boolean retrieval count as "ranking" at all?
drills.a: Boolean retrieval evaluates a match/no-match expression (AND/OR/NOT) with no relevance scale -- documents either satisfy the expression or don't, ordered by date/ID, not relevance. There's no way to express "somewhat relevant."

drills.q: Explain vocabulary mismatch precisely with an example, and what dense retrieval trades away to fix it.
drills.a: BM25 scores purely on shared tokens; "car" scores zero against a document that only says "automobile" despite being relevant. Dense embeddings fix this by mapping both to nearby vector-space points, but trade away precision on rare/exact tokens the embedding model barely saw in training.

drills.q: A stakeholder asks why "semantic search" still fails on order-number lookups. What's the fix, and why isn't a better embedding model the answer?
drills.a: Pure dense retrieval structurally can't guarantee exact-token recall -- the embedding model has no principled way to prioritize an exact rare-string match over a topically-similar one. The fix is hybrid retrieval (BM25 + dense, fused), not a better embedding model, because the failure is architectural.

drills.q: What's wrong with training an LTR model directly on raw click logs?
drills.a: It bakes in position bias -- users click higher-ranked results more regardless of true relevance, so the model learns to reinforce whatever ranking already existed. Fix with inverse propensity scoring or randomized interleaving to collect unbiased labels.

drills.q: Describe the four-stage cascade architecture (matching -> pre-ranking -> ranking -> mix-ranking) and how it relates to retrieve-then-rerank.
drills.a: Matching does cheap corpus-scale candidate generation; pre-ranking narrows millions to thousands with a lightweight model; ranking scores thousands to tens with the full LTR/neural model; mix-ranking applies business rules (diversity, ad interleave, dedup). It's the same narrow-then-spend-more-compute pattern as retrieve-then-rerank, just with more stages and business features layered on.

drills.q: When is a full learned-to-rank layer the wrong investment, and what should you use instead?
drills.a: When there isn't enough real interaction data -- small catalogs, low traffic, cold-start. A GBDT trained on sparse/synthetic labels overfits; use hand-tuned boosting (weighted BM25 + recency + popularity) instead, which is transparent and effective at that scale.

drills.q: Why can LLM-based query rewriting (HyDE, keyword expansion) hurt some queries while helping others?
drills.a: It can distort the original intent or overamplify rare terms the user never cared about for certain query types, while genuinely helping others (conversational follow-ups, typo-heavy input). It needs per-query-type evaluation, never blanket adoption.

drills.q: Design the ranking stack for a marketplace search product with natural-language queries, exact SKU lookups, and sponsored listings as a monetization objective.
drills.a: Hybrid retrieval (BM25 for SKU/brand exact lookups, dense for paraphrased queries) fused with RRF. Cross-encoder reranks the fused top-100 to a top-20-40 shortlist. An LTR model (LambdaMART baseline) reorders using relevance + CTR + conversion + price + inventory + personalization, trained with propensity-corrected labels. Sponsored listings interleave as a separate mix-ranking step, not blended into the LTR score, to preserve auditability.

drills.q: Would you train one unified end-to-end ranking model instead of a staged retrieval -> rerank -> LTR pipeline? Why or why not?
drills.a: A single end-to-end model is tempting but sacrifices debuggability and the ability to independently audit each stage (e.g. proving sponsored placement doesn't bias organic relevance). Staged systems remain the practical default specifically because of that auditability requirement at real business complexity.

drills.q: A candidate says "reranking and learned-to-rank are basically the same thing." What's the correction?
drills.a: A cross-encoder reranker optimizes text relevance alone via joint attention over the query-document pair. LTR optimizes a business objective using a broader feature set (which can include the reranker's own score as one input) plus signals like CTR, price, and personalization that no text-similarity model can see -- they answer different questions.
